memory_update.text: Pure-play voting-equipment and ballot-logistics companies are largely private; public equity exposure is mostly adjacent through govtech platforms, cybersecurity/CDN, identity verification, and government-services contractors.
TYL should remain a reference candidate for election-administration workflows because Tyler explicitly markets election-worker disbursements and has broad state/local government penetration.
NET is the clearest public election-cybersecurity reference name due to Cloudflare's Athenian Project for state and local election websites, but monetization/purity requires verification.
PSN belongs in the underfollowed lane as a possible election-critical-infrastructure cyber contractor; require direct contract evidence before promoting beyond hypothesis.
MITK is a speculative shadow candidate for election identity workflows; verify any secretary-of-state, voter-registration, ballot-request, petition, or election-vendor integrations.
NET is a high-attention reference anchor for election-website cybersecurity via Cloudflare's Athenian Project; useful benchmark, not the underfollowed alpha lane.
TLS is an underfollowed small-cap candidate for public-sector cyber/identity/GRC exposure, but direct election-agency evidence remains unverified.
IDN is a speculative micro-cap identity-verification candidate; direct election use must be verified before it survives later Serenity layers.
GAHC/GES is a speculative OTC micro-cap direct election-services trace, but asset-sale disclosures may remove or dilute the exposure.

Core US voting-system vendors such as major voting-machine, ballot-marking, and election-management-system providers appear mostly private; future passes should map private vendors to public suppliers, equipment, software, mail, cybersecurity, and certified component dependencies.

The more investable public chokepoints may sit one layer away from voting machines: DDoS/WAF/CDN, identity verification, cyber GRC, mail-ballot automation, printing/inserting/sorting equipment, secure hosting, and state/local procurement integrators.

Direct voting-machine exposure is mostly private; public-market work should focus on adjacent govtech, election-results reporting, cyber/identity, print/mail logistics, and micro-cap exceptions only with strict filing verification.
TYL is the strongest public reference candidate for election-administration adjacency, but the exposure is buried in broader state/local govtech and requires county-level contract mapping.
TLS is a small-cap underfollowed hypothesis for election cybersecurity/identity workflows; no direct election contract was verified in this pass.
GAHC is a speculative micro-cap exception with direct historical election-services language, but 2026 asset-sale filings may have removed most operating exposure.

Election-infrastructure spend likely fragments across state and local agencies, creating discovery potential in maintenance contracts, secure reporting tools, identity verification, mail-ballot workflow vendors, and cyber-hardening contractors rather than only voting machines.

Direct certified voting-system manufacturers in the US market appear mostly private or embedded; public-market mapping should emphasize adjacent chokepoints such as public-sector software, cyber GRC, identity, secure records, source-code escrow, equipment lifecycle, and mail/ballot logistics.

TLS should remain in the underfollowed lane as a small-cap cyber/identity government contractor, but it requires direct election-office or state/local election-security procurement evidence before upgrading beyond hypothesis.

IRM is a hidden-adjacent candidate because it explicitly markets election-security lifecycle services; later layers must test materiality because election services may be immaterial versus its broader records/data-center business.

CISA and EAC evidence supports treating election infrastructure as a regulated/certified critical-infrastructure procurement node, but current public-company exposure is likely fragmented and indirect.

node: Election administration, voting infrastructure, and election cybersecurity
summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Layer 1B expansion found few pure-play US-listed election infrastructure vendors because core voting-system assets such as ES&S, Hart InterCivic, Clear Ballot, Democracy Live, Runbeck, Civix, Pro V&V, and SLI Compliance appear private or embedded. The public-market map therefore shifts toward adjacent direct enablers: state/local government software platforms, election website cybersecurity/CDN, government cyber/critical-infrastructure contractors, and identity-verification vendors. The strongest direct evidence among US-listed names is Cloudflare's election-specific Athenian Project and Tyler Technologies' explicit public-sector/election-worker payment workflow. Parsons and Mitek are included as underfollowed/speculative adjacent nodes requiring contract-level verification before promotion. Expanded the election administration / election cybersecurity node through a scarce-supplier lens. Direct public-market exposure is limited because core voting-system vendors are often private, but plausible US-public candidates exist in adjacent chokepoints: election-website DDoS/WAF/CDN protection, public-sector cyber/identity compliance, authoritative ID verification workflows, and a highly speculative OTC direct election-services asset. No buy/sell view is implied. Under the election administration node, the cleanest direct voting-machine vendors appear mostly private, so the US-listed expansion set should emphasize adjacent public-sector software, election-results publishing, cyber/identity/secure-network contractors, and very small election-service assets.
